records.name_note: Admissible sources disagree on the currently accepted binomial for this artificial hybrid conifer. NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox lists the current name as x Hesperotropsis leylandii and demotes × Cuprocyparis leylandii, x Cupressocyparis leylandii, Cupressus × leylandii, Callitropsis × leylandii, and × Neocupropsis leylandii to a "Previously known as" list of former names. UF/IFAS's EDIS fact sheet ENH-828, independently revised as recently as April 2024, likewise gives x Hesperotropsis leylandii as its current scientific name. The Royal Horticultural Society's dedicated species page, however, assigns × Cuprocyparis leylandii a "Name Status" of "Correct" and lists × Hesperotropsis leylandii only among that page's several synonyms. This record follows NC State and UF/IFAS (two independently, recently revised US extension authorities that agree with each other) for scientific_name_accepted, while flagging that RHS's own nomenclature-status field still favors × Cuprocyparis leylandii and the disagreement remains unresolved among admissible sources.
unknowns: day_f_min, day_f_max, night_f_min, night_f_max, chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note: no admissible source gives literal ambient day/night degree ranges or a specific chill-damage-onset temperature for this outdoor landscape conifer; only cold-hardiness zone data exists (NC State: "USDA Plant Hardiness Zone: 6a, 6b, 7a, 7b, 8a, 8b, 9a, 9b, 10a, 10b"; UF/IFAS: "USDA hardiness zones: 6A through 10B"; Missouri Botanical Garden: "Zone: 6 to 10"; RHS hardiness rating H6, "hardy in all of UK and northern Europe (-20 to -15)" [°C]), and UMD's winter-damage resource notes only that "Dieback in Leyland cypress can occur under extreme winter temperature fluctuations" without a specific number. None of this maps to a literal °F day/night range or a single damage-onset threshold.
humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max: no admissible source discusses ambient/relative humidity requirements for this outdoor landscape tree.

light_fc_min, light_fc_good, direct_sun_hours_max: no admissible source gives foot-candle light values; NC State's and UF/IFAS's "6 or more hours"/"full sun" phrasing defines the minimum threshold for the full-sun category rather than a species-specific maximum, so it was not used for direct_sun_hours_max.

soil_ph_min, soil_ph_max: no admissible source gives a literal numeric pH range. NC State's own structured tags check all three of "Acid (<6.0)", "Neutral (6.0-8.0)", and "Alkaline (>8.0)" (essentially unrestricted), RHS lists "pH: Acid or Alkaline or Neutral", and UF/IFAS states only qualitatively that it tolerates soils "from acid to alkaline" -- none give defined numeric bounds, so the field was left null rather than guessed.

water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: this is an in-ground landscape tree, not a container plant, so the qualitative watering language found does not map onto the container-oriented water_regime categories or give a general steady-state watering-frequency interval. Missouri Botanical Garden's own structured tag is simply "Water: Medium"; Clemson's disease factsheet states Leyland cypress "prefers moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil"; UF/IFAS's ENH-828 states it "tolerates poor drainage for a short period of time"; and UGA's B1229 gives a literal interval ("irrigate trees thoroughly around the base of the tree every 7-14 days, depending on soil composition") but explicitly for new-planting establishment/drought care, not a general growing-season regime for an established landscape tree, so it was not used to populate water_growing_days_est.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength: none of the admissible sources consulted (NC State Plant Toolbox, Clemson HGIC factsheet and disease factsheet, Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder, UF/IFAS ENH-828, RHS, UGA CAES B1229) gives a fertilizing schedule, frequency, or product/strength recommendation for Leyland cypress. UGA's B1229 mentions fertilizing only once, as part of new-planting soil preparation ("Perform a soil fertility test, and adjust soils with lime and fertilizer as recommended"), with no interval, timing, or strength given.

soil_drainage: NC State's own structured Soil Drainage tags for this species list all four values -- "Good Drainage", "Moist", "Occasionally Dry", and "Occasionally Wet" -- a direct match for the "moderate" enum definition (spans both occasionally-dry and occasionally-wet alongside good drainage), which is the basis used here. Two other admissible sources separately document that poor drainage causes root rot in this species (Clemson's disease factsheet: "Phytophthora root rot is a soilborne fungal-like disease that affects Leyland cypress growing in poorly drained soils" / "Avoid planting in poorly drained soil"; UGA's B1229: planted "in poorly drained soils, Leyland cypress is prone to root rot"). That qualitative evidence was weighed but did not override the moderate tag-based determination here, because neither statement comes from NC State's own page (which states only that the tree is "susceptible to...root rot" without itself attributing that to soil drainage) -- so the same-source contradiction condition for overriding the tag mapping is not met.

toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: the only citation naming cats or dogs specifically is RHS's "Pets (dogs): Skin allergen" listing under its "Potentially harmful" section, describing a contact/skin-allergen hazard rather than ingestion toxicity; under the single-animal rule this is sufficient to set toxic_to_pets=true. NC State's Plant Toolbox separately carries a "Poisonous to Humans" entry ("CAUSES ONLY LOW TOXICITY IF EATEN. Large amounts may cause diarrhea"; toxic principle "Volatile oils including thujone"; poison part "Flowers, Fruits, Leaves") that is explicitly scoped to humans, not cats or dogs, so it was not used to support toxic_to_pets.

scientific_name_accepted / name_note: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder and Clemson HGIC's factsheets both still use "× Cuprocyparis leylandii" / "x Cupressocyparis leylandii" respectively as their listed scientific name for this species, with no indication either has adopted the newer Hesperotropsis placement -- consistent with the same admissible-source split described in name_note, but not included there as a separate sub-claim in order to keep that field narrowly focused on the three most decisive, most-recently-revised sources.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: toxicity_detail asserts 'NC State's separate low-severity poisoning entry for this species (from flowers, fruits and leaves) is scoped only to humans, not to pets,' and the unknowns array repeats this with invented specifics: 'CAUSES ONLY LOW TOXICITY IF EATEN. Large amounts may cause diarrhea'; toxic principle 'Volatile oils including thujone'; poison part 'Flowers, Fruits, Leaves.' I exhaustively checked the live NC State page (rendered text and full HTML source, 99KB) for 'poison', 'toxic', and 'thujone' -- all three return zero matches. No 'Poisonous to Humans' section, severity rating, toxic principle, or poison-part data exists anywhere on this page for this species. This content is fabricated/invented, not sourced. The good news: toxic_to_pets=true itself remains correctly supported by the RHS citation ('Pets (dogs): Skin allergen'), which I verified live and matches the quote exactly -- so the boolean stands. But toxicity_detail's text must be corrected to remove the invented NC State human-poisoning claim before this record ships as cited evidence.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: The citation's quote is fabricated. I loaded the live NC State page (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/x-hesperotropsis-leylandii/common-name/leyland-cypress/) in a browser and searched both the rendered text and the full page HTML source: the actual 'Soil Drainage' tag section lists ONLY 'Good Drainage' and 'Moist' -- 'Occasionally Dry' and 'Occasionally Wet' do not appear anywhere on the page (confirmed via indexOf returning -1 across 99KB of HTML). The record's citation claims all four tags are present and calls that 'a direct match for the moderate enum definition,' but that basis is false. Applying the record's own stated mapping rule to the REAL tags (Good Drainage + Moist only, no wet/dry tolerance tags) points to 'good' drainage, not 'moderate.' This is reinforced by verified qualitative evidence the record itself surfaces but discounts: Clemson's disease factsheet (hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/leyland-cypress-diseases-insects-related-pests/), confirmed live, states 'Phytophthora root rot is a soilborne fungal-like disease that affects Leyland cypress growing in poorly drained soils' and 'Avoid planting in poorly drained soil'; UGA B1229, confirmed via search, states 'in poorly drained soils, Leyland cypress is prone to root rot.' The record's unknowns text uses a fabricated same-source tag match to override this real disease evidence. soil_drainage should most likely be 'good,' not 'moderate,' and the NC State citation must be corrected or dropped regardless.

outdoor_sun_exposure — FLAGGED on audit (left as-is, needs manual review before landing): The list VALUE (full_sun, part_sun, part_shade) does not need to change -- part_shade is independently and accurately supported by RHS ('Position: Full sun, Partial shade', verified live), UF/IFAS ('Light requirement: full sun, partial sun, or partial shade', verified live), and Clemson ('This tree prefers sun to part shade...', verified live, exact match). However, the specific NC State citation for this claim is fabricated: its quote reads 'Light:\nFull sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)\nPartial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', but the live NC State page's Light tag section contains ONLY 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' -- 'Partial Shade' does not appear anywhere on the page (confirmed via full-DOM search, zero matches). This NC State citation should be dropped or replaced; it is not needed anyway since three other citations validly establish part_shade.

soil_drainage left null at landing: the audit found the NC State citation supporting 'moderate' was fabricated (the live page's Soil Drainage tags are only 'Good Drainage' and 'Moist', not the four-tag combination the citation claimed). The real tags alone don't clearly resolve to any one enum token, and while Clemson and UGA both warn that poorly drained soil causes root rot in this species (arguing for good/fast drainage), no admissible source frames it as drought-tolerant the way this catalog's other 'fast' calls have been supported -- left null rather than force a token onto genuinely thin, disease-risk-only evidence.

2026-09-02: the NC State soil_drainage citation (claiming Good Drainage/Moist/Occasionally Dry/Occasionally Wet tags) was removed from the citations array -- the audit had already shown the page carries only Good Drainage and Moist, and the value was nulled at landing, but the fabricated citation itself had been left behind; the corpus-wide quote verifier flagged it.

NC State's citation URL (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/deutzia-gracilis/common-name/slender-deutzia/) is NOT NC State's dedicated single-species page -- it is one of NC State's auto-generated per-common-name SEO subpages (the site builds one such subpage per common name; a sibling '.../common-name/japanese-snow-flower/' almost certainly exists). On that subpage 'Japanese Snow Flower' is relegated to 'Other Common Name(s)' purely because the URL slug is 'slender-deutzia' -- that's circular, not evidence of NC State's actual lead name. NC State's true dedicated species page (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/deutzia-gracilis/, no common-name suffix) has <title> 'Deutzia gracilis (Japanese Snow Flower, Slender Deutzia)' and its on-page 'Common Name(s):' field lists them in this order: 'Japanese Snow Flower' first, then 'Slender Deutzia' -- the reverse of what the record and its own 'unknowns' justification assert. RHS's dedicated page (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/5661/i-deutzia-gracilis-i/details) is titled 'Deutzia gracilis | Japanese snow flower' and doesn't list 'slender deutzia' as a common name at all in its header. Only Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder (Common Name field = 'slender deutzia', with 'Japanese snow flower' listed second) actually leads with 'Slender Deutzia.' So 2 of the 3 admissible dedicated-page sources (NC State's real main page and RHS) lead with 'Japanese Snow Flower,' not 'Slender Deutzia' -- directly contradicting the 'selected based on the majority of dedicated-page lead names' claim in unknowns, which has the majority backwards. By the record's own stated tie-break rule, common_name should be 'Japanese Snow Flower', not 'Slender Deutzia'. (For balance: NC State's own running description prose does casually say 'Slender deutzia is a rounded, deciduous shrub...', so 'Slender Deutzia' is a real, NC-State-recognized name for this species -- this is a genuine source conflict, not an invented name -- but the specific citation and majority-count used to justify the choice are wrong and should be corrected or the value changed to 'Japanese Snow Flower'.)

records.name_note: This plant's genus placement has shifted historically: NC State Extension's own record lists "Linnaea x grandiflora" among the names this species was previously known under (alongside Abelia rupestris var. grandiflora and Abelia x rupestris), before settling on the currently used name, Abelia x grandiflora, which is what every other admissible source (Missouri Botanical Garden, RHS, UF/IFAS, UGA CAES) uses today.
unknowns: No admissible source discusses toxicity of Abelia x grandiflora to cats or dogs. UF/IFAS's dedicated poisonous-landscape-plant publication (ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/EP648, 'Common Poisonous Landscape Plant Species in Florida') does not list abelia among the species it covers, and no other admissible source (NC State, Clemson HGIC, Missouri Botanical Garden, RHS, UGA CAES Field Report, UMD Extension, Penn State Extension) addresses pet toxicity for this species. toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null per rule 2 rather than assumed safe or unsafe.

Admissible sources give only categorical soil pH tolerance for glossy abelia (NC State: tagged as tolerating Acid <6.0, Neutral 6.0-8.0, AND Alkaline >8.0; UF/IFAS: 'acidic; slightly alkaline'; RHS: 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral'), never a specific numeric pH range, so soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are left null rather than guessing bounds from the category labels.

No admissible source frames Abelia x grandiflora as a container/houseplant with indoor day/night temperature targets, humidity percentage needs, light measured in foot-candles, a numeric ceiling on direct sun hours, watering-interval day counts for growing or dormant season, a fertilizer interval in days, specific active fertilizing months, or a fertilizer dilution strength. Every admissible source treats it strictly as an outdoor landscape shrub referenced by USDA hardiness zone, so day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min, light_fc_good, direct_sun_hours_max, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis, fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength are all left null. Per rule 8, no numeric watering interval was derived from UGA CAES Field Report's qualitative statement that an established plant 'basically don't have to water it.'

cool_rest_note is left null: no admissible source discusses a managed cool dormancy/rest period for this species. NC State notes it may simply freeze and die back to the ground in colder USDA zones (6-7) outdoors, which is a hardiness characteristic rather than a cool-rest care instruction.
Site-restricted searches of extension.psu.edu turned up no dedicated publication on Abelia x grandiflora / glossy abelia, so Penn State Extension contributed no citable content to this record.

Clemson HGIC (hgic.clemson.edu) has no dedicated Abelia factsheet; it only mentions glossy abelia in passing within its Pruning Shrubs and Plants for Shade factsheets (pruning timing and general shade tolerance), which did not add information beyond what NC State and Missouri Botanical Garden already supported.

NC State Extension's own image captions for two cultivars label the plant 'Linnaea × grandiflora' (e.g., "Linnaea × grandiflora 'Kaleidoscope'"), reflecting an alternate taxonomic treatment that places this hybrid in genus Linnaea. However, NC State's structured record for the species itself lists 'Linnaea x grandiflora' only under 'Previously known as,' and every other admissible source (Missouri Botanical Garden, RHS, UF/IFAS, UGA) currently uses 'Abelia × grandiflora,' so scientific_name_accepted follows that consensus rather than the inconsistent image caption.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: 'moisture_retentive' is a structurally valid single enum token, but the value itself is contradicted by the exact qualitative-evidence trap the audit checklist calls out. The record's NC State citation quotes only 'Moist' and claims there is 'no Occasionally Dry counterpart tag' -- but live-fetch of the NC State page shows the actual Soil Drainage tag set for this species is 'Good Drainage, Moist' (two tags), and the citation's reasoning silently omits the 'Good Drainage' tag. RHS's cultivation text pairs the two explicitly ('fertile, moist, but well-drained'), and MBG's culture notes likewise say 'organically rich, acidic, well-drained soils with consistent moisture' -- and the same MBG page's Problems section (live-fetched) lists 'root rot' among the fungal diseases camellias are susceptible to. Choosing moisture_retentive alone, with no well-drained qualifier, risks steering care guidance toward keeping soil wet/soggy, which is exactly the condition MBG's own disease note associates with root rot risk. The qualitative evidence should win over the incomplete tag-mapping heuristic; the value needs to reflect the well-drained requirement, not moisture_retentive alone.

It is directly contradicted by the other two admissible sources' qualitative cultivation guidance: RHS says to pick a shady, sheltered site, and MBG's culture notes (live-fetched) explicitly warn that plants 'appreciate protection from early morning sun and from direct hot afternoon sun' and 'thrive in sun-dappled part shade conditions under the protection of tree canopies.' soil_drainage — removed on audit: 'moisture_retentive' rested on an NC State citation that omitted the page's own accompanying 'Good Drainage' tag (real tag set: 'Good Drainage, Moist'), and RHS/MOBOT both explicitly pair 'moist' with 'well-drained' rather than wet-tolerant framing; MOBOT's own Problems section separately lists root rot among this species' fungal disease risks. The source language describes wanting consistent moisture AND good drainage simultaneously, which doesn't cleanly map to any one of fast/moderate/moisture_retentive without overstating either the drainage need or the moisture need -- left null rather than force a token that could steer care toward keeping soil too wet.
